design_detail: Cross-sectional quantitative PET study (Neuropsychopharmacology 2005;30:1741-1750) in which 23 people abstinent from MDMA and 19 people who had never used it were each scanned twice on the same day, about 135 min apart, with two serotonin transporter radioligands, [11C]McN5652 and [11C]DASB, using arterial blood sampling and a single-tissue compartment model. Three binding measures were compared in 15 regions of interest drawn on co-registered MRI by a neurologist blind to group: total distribution volume (DV), specific distribution volume (DVspec, regional DV minus cerebellar DV) and the ratio (DVR).
can_establish: That in this sample, binding of both radioligands was lower on average in the group abstinent from MDMA, with the largest and most consistent differences in neocortical regions, and that the two tracers agreed closely within the same people.
cannot_establish: That MDMA caused the difference (one scan per person, no pre-use measure, more other-drug use in the MDMA group); that the difference means loss of nerve terminals rather than lower transporter expression; that people with lighter exposure are affected (the group had used on average 97 occasions); or that transporters recover with abstinence, which is tested here only as a correlation across different people, with one-tailed tests.

sample.recruitment: Advertisements in newspapers, fliers, radio and the internet, and word of mouth from previous participants; telephone screen, then face-to-face assessment with the SCID-IV, physical examination, blood chemistry and drug screens (pp. 1742-1743).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: MDMA group: use on at least 25 separate occasions; comparison group: never used MDMA. Both groups could have used other recreational drugs but none in the 2 weeks before the study. Excluded: psychiatric disorders in which serotonin has been implicated, past or present alcohol use disorder, current drug dependence; negative urine and blood drug screens other than cannabis (p. 1742).
sample.demographics: MDMA group 10 women, 13 men, mean age 22.04 years, 13.7 years of education; comparison group 11 women, 8 men, mean age 26, 13.68 years of education (Table 1, p. 1744). No standard deviations or tests are given for age or education.
sample.attrition: Not reported; both scans were obtained in all 42 participants (one group's data for some 'other drug' items are based on 22 of 23).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers answering advertisements for a study of ecstasy; the MDMA group had used the drug on average 97 times, so the findings describe people at the heavier end of recreational use. The comparison group had far less experience of other drugs, so group membership tracks a general pattern of drug use, not MDMA alone.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported drug history at telephone and face-to-face screening; urine and blood drug screens for current drugs only; no hair analysis (p. 1742).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Mean 96.96 MDMA exposures (range 28-324) over 2.97 (SD 2.2) years; 3.12 (1.59) exposures per month; usual dose 1.79 (0.49) tablets, maximum dose 5.83 (3.92) tablets (Table 1, p. 1744). Route not stated; tablet content not verified.
exposure.polysubstance: The MDMA group used more of every other drug class: cannabis 96% vs 37% lifetime, hallucinogens 83% vs 11%, cocaine 52% vs 5%, opioids 43% vs 5%, other stimulants 48% vs 5%, ketamine 57% vs 0%, alcohol 100% vs 79%, tobacco 87% vs 67% (Table 1, p. 1744). The authors state that matching on other drugs proved impossible and that an effect of other drugs cannot be excluded (p. 1748).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 weeks of self-reported abstinence from all illicit drugs, with negative urine and blood screens (cannabis exempted); mean time since last MDMA 4.74 months (SD 8.71) (Table 1, p. 1744).

comparison.controls: 19 people recruited the same way who reported never using MDMA (p. 1742).
comparison.matching: Described as well matched for age and education; no statistical test is given, and the mean ages differ by about 4 years (22.0 vs 26.0).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan; the paper notes that an unidentified condition predisposing to drug use could contribute to the reductions (p. 1748).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Lower on every class (Table 1, p. 1744); 37% had used cannabis, 11% hallucinogens, 5% cocaine.

outcomes.instruments: [11C]McN5652 and [11C]DASB PET (GE Advance, axial resolution 5.8 mm), 95-min dynamic scans with arterial input function corrected for metabolites; single-tissue compartment model; 15 regions of interest drawn on MRI by a neurologist blind to group; cerebellum as reference region for DVspec and DVR (pp. 1742-1743).
outcomes.validity_norms: Both tracers are serotonin transporter ligands validated in baboons; the authors note that PET measures underestimate transporter loss measured in vitro, being about half of it in baboons (p. 1748). No normative values.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Neurotoxicity' is operationalized as lower regional binding; recovery as a positive correlation between global binding and months since last use.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 15 preplanned regional comparisons for each of 3 binding measures and 2 tracers, plus correlational analyses with use variables, are reported without adjustment (pp. 1743, 1745).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The neurologist who drew the regions was blind to group, worked from MRI anatomy, and viewed PET images normalized to their own maximum (p. 1743).

analysis.effect_sizes: ANOVA main effect of group: [11C]McN5652 DV F=5.3 (p=0.028), DVspec F=6.6 (p=0.014), DVR F=5.9 (p=0.02); [11C]DASB DV F=4.1 (p=0.05), DVspec F=5.0 (p=0.031), DVR F=7.4 (p=0.01); no group-by-region interaction for either tracer (p=0.16 to 0.45) (Table 2, p. 1746). Regional percent differences in DVspec (Table 3, p. 1748; editors' calculation of standardized differences from the printed means and SDs, Hedges g with 95% interval): [11C]DASB occipital cortex -68% (g -2.16, -2.98 to -1.43), temporal -48% (-2.06, -2.86 to -1.33), parietal -51% (-1.83, -2.60 to -1.13), dorsolateral prefrontal -55% (-1.64, -2.38 to -0.96), hippocampus -40% (-1.26, -1.96 to -0.62), thalamus -23% (-0.62, -1.26 to -0.01), midbrain -21% (-0.48, -1.11 to 0.13), caudate -14% (-0.40, -1.03 to 0.20), putamen -13% (-0.35, -0.97 to 0.26). Correlations (one-tailed): global [11C]McN5652 DVspec with months of abstinence r=0.418, p=0.026; DVR with abstinence r=0.494, p<0.010; global DVR with typical monthly dose r=0.38 and 0.37 for the two tracers, p=0.04 (described in the text as inverse) (p. 1745).
analysis.covariates: None: no adjustment for age, sex, education or other drug use.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 15 regions are shown for DVspec (Table 3) and plotted for all three measures (Figure 4); the DV and DVR tables are not printed, and the counts of significant regions appear only in the text.
analysis.power: Not formally reported; the authors state the study was not powered to demonstrate correlations between binding and use variables and call those analyses preliminary (p. 1748).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Group means of serotonin transporter binding were lower in the MDMA group with both tracers and all three binding measures, most clearly in neocortical regions and hippocampus, with substantial overlap of individual values and no group-by-region interaction; and binding was higher in people who had been abstinent longer, in a correlation across people tested one-tailed.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that the data provide "strong evidence of reduced SERT density" in some people who use MDMA recreationally, and that exploratory analyses suggested that transporter measures recover with time (abstract, p. 1741). The Discussion calls MDMA-induced toxicity 'the most parsimonious explanation' (p. 1746). The design is cross-sectional with large differences in other drug use, the recovery analysis compares different people at a single time point, and the authors themselves list pre-existing differences and other drugs as unexcluded (p. 1748).

timeline.event: The same group's first PET study with [11C]McN5652 reported a large global reduction (McCann et al., Lancet 352:1433-1437), which this paper describes as having had high variability and needing logarithmic transformation.
Follow-up by the same group in 16 people, again with [11C]DASB, reporting cortical and hippocampal reductions and no striatal change (McCann et al., Psychopharmacology 200:439-450); not read here.
Independent replication in 49 people with hair verification: cortical and hippocampal reductions, normal striatum
Independent study finding reductions in neocortex, pallidostriatum and amygdala, with a dose relation
Independent study with arterial input and a selective 5-HT2A tracer: lower cortical binding, higher 5-HT2A binding
No difference in men abstinent for at least a year

replication.where_it_stands: The cortical finding has been reproduced by three independent laboratories with the same tracer; the subcortical findings have not been consistent, and this study's thalamic reduction was not found by the Toronto or New York groups.

funding.funder: US Public Health Service grants DA10217 (McCann), AA11653 (Szabo), DA00206 (Ricaurte) and NCRR grant M01RR002719 (Acknowledgements, p. 1749).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state that none has a financial or other conflict of interest that might bias the work (p. 1749).
funding.affiliations_note: Johns Hopkins; the same laboratory published the 1998 PET study and the 2002 primate report later retracted (Ricaurte et al., 2002), which is a reason for close reading rather than to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A study of the same people scanned before first use and repeatedly through use and abstinence, with biological verification of exposure and a comparison group with the same other-drug use, plus a measure that can distinguish lower transporter expression from loss of terminals.

domains.note: The MDMA group used every other drug class far more often, and no analysis adjusts for this or for the 4-year age difference; age lowers transporter binding, which here runs against the finding, while other stimulant and hallucinogen use runs with it.
Exposure, dose and abstinence are self-reported; no hair analysis; tablet content unverified; the standard deviation of time since last use (8.71 months) is nearly twice its mean.
Volunteers answering advertisements for a study of ecstasy, with a comparison group of people with much less drug experience; no pre-use measurement.
Both scans in all participants; a few self-report items missing for one person.
Quantitative PET with arterial input, two tracers in the same people, blinded region drawing; cortical signal is small and noisy, which the authors discuss.

Ninety regional comparisons without correction; correlations tested one-tailed on a stated directional hypothesis; the significance counts for DV are given only in the text and differ from those for DVR and DVspec.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The imaging is of high technical quality, but the comparison is between groups that differ in every drug class and in age, with self-reported exposure and no correction for 90 comparisons. It supports a group difference in transporter binding, strongest in cortex; it cannot support a causal or quantitative statement, and its recovery analysis is a between-person correlation with one-tailed tests.

key_findings.finding: Main effect of group on binding was significant for both tracers and all three binding measures (DV, DVspec, DVR): [11C]McN5652 F=5.3 (p=0.028), 6.6 (p=0.014), 5.9 (p=0.02); [11C]DASB F=4.1 (p=0.05), 5.0 (p=0.031), 7.4 (p=0.01); no group-by-region interaction.
Preplanned regional comparisons of DV were significant in 12 of 15 regions for [11C]McN5652 and 9 of 15 for [11C]DASB; with DVR and DVspec, 10 of 15 regions for both tracers.
key_findings.note: No correction for 15 comparisons; the interaction term that would license regional comparisons was not significant.

key_findings.finding: Percent differences in DVspec with [11C]DASB were largest in cortex: occipital -68%, dorsolateral prefrontal -55%, parietal -51%, temporal -48%, hippocampus -40%, and smallest in putamen (-13%), caudate (-14%) and midbrain (-21%); the [11C]McN5652 pattern was the same (occipital -54%, putamen -20%).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation of standardized differences from the printed means and SDs (Hedges g, 95% interval): occipital -2.16 (-2.98 to -1.43), temporal -2.06 (-2.86 to -1.33), parietal -1.83 (-2.60 to -1.13), hippocampus -1.26 (-1.96 to -0.62), thalamus -0.62 (-1.26 to -0.01), midbrain -0.48 (-1.11 to 0.13), caudate -0.40 (-1.03 to 0.20), putamen -0.35 (-0.97 to 0.26).

key_findings.finding: Global [11C]McN5652 binding was higher in people with longer abstinence (DVspec r=0.418, p=0.026; DVR r=0.494, p<0.010), and global DVR was lower with higher typical monthly dose (r printed as 0.38 and 0.37, described as inverse; p=0.04 for both tracers).
key_findings.locator: Results, last paragraph ('Exploratory analyses evaluating a possible relationship…')
key_findings.note: One-tailed tests on a directional hypothesis, across different people at one time point, in a sample the authors say was not powered for these analyses (p. 1748).

key_findings.finding: Binding of the two radioligands agreed closely: across regions overall r=0.97 (controls 0.96, MDMA group 0.98), and within individual participants overall r=0.55.
Group means of the delivery parameter K1 did not differ ([11C]DASB F=1.68, p=0.125; [11C]McN5652 F=1.599, p=0.162), so differences in tracer delivery do not explain the binding difference.

The MDMA group had used MDMA on average 97 times (range 28-324) over about 3 years, at a usual dose of 1.79 tablets and a maximum of 5.83, and had last used it a mean of 4.74 months (SD 8.71) earlier.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives mean ages of 22.04 (MDMA group) and 26 (comparison group) with no standard deviations and no test, while the text states that the groups were well matched for age.
reporting_issues.consequence: A 4-year age difference is not negligible for a measure that declines with age; here it would bias towards higher binding in the MDMA group, so it does not explain the finding, but the claim of matching is not supported by a test.

reporting_issues.issue: Correlations between binding and typical monthly dose are described in the text as inverse while the coefficients are printed as positive (r=0.38 and 0.37).
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction has to be taken from the text; the sign of the printed coefficients is wrong or the word 'inversely' is.

reporting_issues.issue: The percent differences in Table 3 are printed without signs although every value is a reduction, and the table's title prints the tracer as '[11C]McN56652'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographic; the direction is unambiguous from the means, but values copied from this table can be reported with the wrong sign, as happens in later reviews.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints one cell of the ANOVA as '1.4 (0 = 0.25)' instead of a p-value.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor misprint; the corresponding DV and DVR cells give p=0.25.

reporting_issues.issue: Regional comparisons were run although the stated condition for them (a significant group-by-region interaction, or a main effect) was met only by the main effect, and 90 comparisons across regions, measures and tracers are reported without correction; the correlations are one-tailed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pattern of significant regions, and the two correlations near p=0.03 to 0.04, are less secure than the printed p-values suggest; the cortical differences are large enough to survive, the subcortical ones are not.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that reductions were found 'in selected cortical and subcortical structures' and that measures recover with time, without noting that the abstinence analysis is a between-person correlation with one-tailed tests in a sample the Discussion says was underpowered for it.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader taking the abstract alone would take recovery as observed in people over time.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 1741-1750 (all pages; Tables 1-3 read in the text extraction, Figure 4 panels not read numerically)
